newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton rates seen easing in Pakistan, India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton rates seen easing in Pakistan, India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to ease in the next week in Pakistan and India because of new crop arrivals, dealers in the two countries said on Friday.
In Pakistan, rates fell after monsoon rains lifted prospects for output in the southern province of Sindh, dealer Nasim Usman said.
He said rains in the leading producing province of Punjab would also benefit the crop, with dealers expecting a yield of about 10 million 375-lb bales, equal to the target set by the government.
The private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) on Friday fixed the rate of the 1997/98 NIAB-78 variety 11.25 rupees lower at 2,560 rupees per maund (37.32).
The 1996/97 crop prices closed steady because of a lack of demand from spinners, who prefer new crop cotton, Usman said.
In the kerb market, the new-crop NIAB-78 was quoted at 2,550/2,560 rupees per maund.
Some 190,080 bales of cotton were registered for export by July 28, the KCA said.
Pakistan shipped 142,212 bales of cotton by July 19 compared to 1.82 million bales a year ago, it said.

In India, traders on Thursday sought early action on a parliamentary committee's suggestion that the government release at least 10 million 170-kg bales of cotton for export ahead of the 1997/98 season beginning in October.
"It's a welcome suggestion and must be implemented immediately, but the export quota should be open to all," said a leading cotton trader.
The committee, which studied the problems of cotton growers, suggested that half the quota be given to the state-run Cotton Corporation of India and the rest to others.
Traders said the government should also announce a long-term policy for cotton exports as India's production was expected to rise in the next few years.
Indian authorities recently announced that a technical mission launched in the current season would help boost productivity in the near future.
According to traders, prospects of the 1997/98 crop, which will come onto the market in October, were bright.
The 1996/97 crop has been estimated at 16.78 million bales, up from the previous year's 16.27 million.
Traders said cotton arrivals indicated that the current year's crop could even touch 17 million bales.
In the week to Thursday, cotton firmed on the local market on a shortage of ready stocks.
Expectations that the government might allow state-owned agencies to export more cotton also aided the trend.
"Some state-owned agencies are nursing unsold stocks and are demanding permission to export more," one broker said.
Traders said India's cotton exports in 1996/97 were expected at 1.4 million bales compared with 790,000 in the previous season.
The government has already released 1.34 million bales for export in the current season, of which 1.15 million have been registered and 900,000 shipped.
India had released 500,000 bales for export before the start of the current season and the move pushed prices up in a market saddled with huge carryover stocks from the previous year.
In spot, Bengal-deshi rose 40/65 rupees to 1,125/1,160 rupees per maund (37.32 kg), Punjab saw-ginned by 25 rupees to 1,830/1,900 and F-414 by 10 to 2,080/2,100.
Among Gujarat varieties, Kalyan cotton gained 300/400 rupees to 14,500/15,100 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and wagad cotton rose 500 rupees to 13,500. Kala-ginned rose 300/400 to 12,700.
"This is just a usual rally at the tail-end of the season and prices may ease in the coming days before the start of the new season," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading dealer.
"In some centres, scattered arrivals of the new crop from early sowing have already commenced," he said. "It is too early to predict the size of the new crop."
"The crop is very satisfactory," Amarsey said.
($1 = 40.62 Pakistani rupees)
-- Bombay Commodities +91-22-265 9000
